narrative:
The model estimates a 70% chance that you will leave your job, meaning you are more likely than not to depart and are therefore treated as a high retention risk. That is why the promotion was denied: the decision reflects concern that the organization may invest in a promotion you are unlikely to stay to use.

The strongest factor was your total work experience. Your six-to-ten years overall made leaving more likely; among employees predicted to stay, about half have only one to five years, while roughly a third have six to ten. The second most influential factor was other job opportunities. You reported none, and this was the one top factor that pushed toward staying, reducing the leave risk, though not enough to offset the stronger signals. The third factor was your one-to-five years with your current organization, which added to the leave signal in your overall profile.

Context such as your master’s degree, 6k–10k salary, no annual bonus, low sense of job stability, and not feeling you received the deserved promotion reinforces the retention concern, though these were less influential. Before promotion is reconsidered, clarify your development and reward expectations, discuss what would make you stay, and request a transparent promotion review. The organization should separate promotion readiness from attrition prediction and avoid treating this estimate as a final judgment.
